title: Why Top Agents Hire a Real Estate Writer
html:
The agents at the top of a market have two things in common: a constant need for written material and very little time available in front of a computer. Production in residential real estate depends on relationships, and relationships are built at listing appointments, inspections, broker caravans and client dinners rather than in front of a keyboard. The writing still needs to be done, which is why the most productive agents hand it to a professional.

A bio is the first piece that many agents choose to outsource. Prospective clients research an agent before the first meeting, and the bio is usually the first thing they read. A bio that lists production figures and designations tells a reader what the agent has done. A bio that explains how the agent works and what a client can expect from the first call tells the reader whether to pick up the phone. A bio should also carry personal elements, because people want to work with someone they can relate to and qualifications vary.

Property descriptions carry more weight than the length would suggest. A seller reads the description of the family home closely and may want to share it with their network. A description that is specific to the house, the street and the surrounding neighborhood shows that the agent invested time and effort into the listing. Buyers want clarity, and the type of information that only the sellers or a local expert would know. A description assembled from the same adjectives as every other listing in the MLS signals the opposite. Sellers notice and negative feedback about an agent can spread quickly.

Market updates, newsletters and process guides build engagement. An agent who sends a monthly note on local inventory and pricing stays in front of past clients, generating a higher potential for referrals. Producing a knowledge-based article means pulling statistics and providing insights on those statistics, and that is time that most agents do not have.

At the brokerage level, a press release can be more effective than an advertisement. Agent awards, new offices, fundraisers and unusual listings are legitimate news to a local business journal or trade outlet. A press release carries more credibility than an advertisement and is also more cost effective.

Agents like to share information with their clients and sphere of influence. Since a press release contains more detail than an advertisement, sharing it is more worthwhile. When agents read a press release about a colleague, it can enhance recruitment efforts put forth by the brokerage.

In the upper tier of the market, the stakes are always higher. Buyers and sellers of luxury homes tend to be highly educated and well connected. Considering the description of an estate may be forwarded among friends, advisors and members of the press, it is easy to see why it should be taken seriously.

The quality of the writing becomes part of the presentation, and the fee for hiring a writer is a small fraction of the commission.

I have been a trusted resource for Berkshire Hathaway HomeServices California Properties since 2008, serving agents across Southern California and the Central Coast. The pitch summaries and editorial frameworks produced for the brokerage have informed features in Robb Report and Mansion Global. Agents and brokerages considering what to hand off are welcome to reach out.

The writing still needs to be done, which is why the most productive agents hand it to a professional.

title: The Role of a LinkedIn Ghostwriter
html:
A managing partner understands the competitive advantage that can be realized from a steady presence on LinkedIn. Business owners and leaders know where their industries are headed better than anyone and, in most cases, they are long on ideas and short on time.

A LinkedIn ghostwriter closes that gap. Depending on the time constraints of the client, the work can begin from a document shared through a notes app, an email or a short, recorded conversation. The writer asks about recent industry developments, the questions that are often raised by clients, the economic trends affecting the practice, and the particular value the firm offers. The answers become the raw material.

From that material, the ghostwriter develops content from the perspective of the client. This includes using the client’s tone, vocabulary, idioms and phrases. A post for a litigator should read differently from a post for a trusts and estates attorney, and both should have a different tone than a post by a real estate broker. The ghostwriter's job is to notice and preserve those differences.

The client reviews each draft before publishing. Drafts are not written in stone, changes are welcome and the appearance of the final version is ultimately up to the client. Review tends to go quickly because the draft is built from the client's ideas instead of a template.

A professional ghostwriter understands how to be discreet when it is necessary. Confidentiality, trade secrets, specific details and any potential discussion that could have a negative impact on the reputation of the client are not included in the article. For attorneys, state bar rules govern what may be said and how it is presented, and the firm's review is the final word.

The result is a consistent presence that reflects real expertise. Connections see the perspective of the client/owner week after week and the level of trust/credibility accumulates.

My work as a ghostwriter has included developing sponsored content for a variety of businesses for the Wilmington Business Journal and ongoing legal content for Ward and Smith, a regional law firm. LinkedIn is the same craft in a shorter form: listen closely, write clearly and let the expert take the credit.

title: How to Start Working with a Ghostwriter
html:
The first conversation with a ghostwriter produces a better outcome when the client brings a few specific ideas. A consistent piece of advice I give to my clients is not to worry about providing too much information. It is truly the more information the better, as it helps me form a more complete picture of the business.

The first objective is to identify the goal of the article. A post aimed at earning referrals from colleagues or advancing recruitment efforts is different from an article meant to reassure a first-time homebuyer. The target audience and the action that is desired from the reader sets the tone before a word is drafted.

The information that is provided is essential for creating an article from the perspective of the client. This could include bullet points in an email, a transcript, industry article or web page. A ghostwriter analyzes the information for sentence length, formality and tone. A recorded conversation can be the entire basis for an article if that is the preference of the client.

Of course, the material forms the basis of the article. Whether it’s a slide deck, meeting notes or just a list of points to make, the facts are vital for guiding the writer. Being specific about the tone, details and direction of the article helps to reduce the number of edits that may be required.

The platform also has a significant impact on the finished product. A newsletter, LinkedIn post, a press release and a website page each have a different set of requirements and conventions, and a piece that was written for a specific platform rarely transfers without reworking.

Deadlines and the expected number of revisions should be included in the initial conversation. It is also helpful to discuss anything that should be excluded, such as proprietary information, trade secrets, pending legal matters, or business strategies. A prudent ghostwriter will ask, but it saves time when the client volunteers.

An email or a short conversation is usually enough to get started, however. The rest can follow as the work settles into a rhythm. I have extensive experience working with clients in real estate, law, finance and technical fields, though I welcome new clients and the research, interview and writing skills are applicable to every industry.

It is truly the more information the better, as it helps me form a more complete picture of the business.

title: What Happens to the Content after the Real Estate Conference Is Over?
html:
An industry conference can be expensive: registration fees, airfare and nights in a hotel are just a few of the costs. Add in lost time and effort, along with the fact that the content is frequently never used, and the return on investment is relatively low. Were the panels on market shifts, luxury marketing and buyer behavior timely and informative? Did the attendees get something out of it?

Who knows, but in most cases the value of that content is gone when the event is over. Why not re-leverage that content?

A conference produces a significant amount of content, including market data, statistics and insights from industry leaders. This content is usually lost unless a trade publication elects to cover the event and even if that happens, the brokerage will not have an opportunity to review the article.

Having a series of articles created from the event that are specifically tailored to a variety of outlets can build engagement with existing and prospective clients. Further, the content can increase recruitment efforts and position the brokerage as an industry leader.

Building the articles is not without its challenges, however. Many choose to upload a recording of the event to transcription software. Because of the potential for inaccuracies, doing so can be negatively impactful to the professional reputation of the brokerage.

The summaries produced by transcription software usually eliminate or gloss over many of the anecdotes, insights and conversational elements that make it worthwhile to attend an in-person event. Transcripts also mangle the details that readers and industry experts will notice, such as the names of neighborhoods and subdivisions, developers and architects.

Regional accents and background noise can result in an entirely different idea than what the speaker intended, and the software will state its guess with full confidence. The bottom line is that it will consistently make errors because it is not able to infer meaning from the context, and it does not do outside research to verify extraneous details.

Real estate speakers will also often include confidential information and use figures of speech. A top producer may use ballpark ideas as estimates or describe a client situation without personally identifying that individual. Someone has to decide what can be published, attribute it correctly and review the figures before anything is published. Fair housing guidelines apply to advertising, and software is unable to judge whether a sentence crosses the line.

One session can become several pieces if handled well. A market panel could be a client-facing article for the brokerage blog, or it could be broken into a series of articles. A condensed version could be the subject of a monthly newsletter or a post for the managing broker's LinkedIn page. Each is written for the target audience and reviewed by the person whose name it carries before publication.

My process starts at the event with in-person attendance. Taking notes, listening carefully and creating recordings adds context and informs the content. Every name, figure and quote is reviewed alongside the recording to ensure the accuracy of the draft. I have written for Berkshire Hathaway HomeServices California Properties since 2008 and have produced conference-based content for a regional law firm since 2021. Brokerages sending a team to a convention or holding a conference are welcome to discuss what the sessions could become.

Add in lost time and effort, along with the fact that the content is frequently never used, and the return on investment is relatively low. Were the panels on market shifts, luxury marketing and buyer behavior timely and informative? Did the attendees get something out of it?

title: Does a Legal Writer Need a Law Degree?
html:
A job post for a legal writer often mentions a JD as a requirement. The reasoning is certainly understandable, as the law is precise and full of unapproachable jargon. The stakes for clients are real, of course, and a careless word can expose the firm to a variety of legal risks.

The requirement combines two different jobs, however. And significantly, the firms that insist on having a writer with a legal degree often pay for a knowledge base that is not required for the role.

Knowing the law is the job of the attorney. Writing is foundational to earning a legal degree and the daily responsibilities of many lawyers, who are often proficient explaining complex, nuanced ideas and crafting dense, careful prose that works in a legal brief.

Making the content engaging and approachable for different audiences is the job of the writer. In an effective thought leadership article, the substance comes from the attorney. The writer adds transitions, conversational elements and research where it is necessary.

The substance originates from the ideas and analysis of the attorney. This can be gathered through interviews, seminar recordings, emails or notes. The attorney reviews each draft before publication. That review is the real safeguard, and no writer's credentials can replace it.

The reason, of course, is that many issues require legal judgment. Some cases and decisions are extremely complicated and can be confusing, even for insiders. Similarly, it can be difficult to determine whether an article drifts from information into advice.

The firm and its compliance department may want to review the article to ensure it complies with state bar requirements pertaining to attorney advertising. A writer with experience in the legal field will know when to ask questions and when outside research may be required.

A writer that is new to the legal field will require more time and effort from the attorney and the firm. Writers with experience in the legal arena typically have a working knowledge of the subject matter and an understanding of how to explain complex ideas in a manner that is approachable for the average person.

I have been a ghostwriter for a regional law firm since 2021 and the process has remained the same: the attorney supplies the substance, I shape it and the attorney signs off before anything is published. The arrangement has relied on this review process instead of a degree and of course, nothing on this page is legal advice.
excerpt: A job post for a legal writer often mentions a JD as a requirement. The reasoning is certainly understandable, as the law is precise and full of unapproachable jargon. The stakes for clients are real, of course, and a careless word can expose the firm to a variety of legal risks.

title: Why Conference Content Needs a Human in the Loop
html:
Transcription software has improved such that it is tempting to treat a conference as a solved problem. Why review the content or hire a writer if it isn’t necessary?

Simply recording the sessions and running the audio through a tool can result in a finished product that appears to be acceptable for a busy professional, at least on a quick review. The sequence can feel efficient; however, it poses a significant risk to the credibility of the firm.

One problem is that transcription software often stumbles on what matters most in professional settings, which is proper names, case names, statutes, acronyms and numbers. A Southern drawl, a Boston vowel or a speaker working in a second language will frequently confuse the technology.

Precise terms may be transformed into different words that sound plausible, which may not appear to be a significant issue at first glance. A small error can become especially problematic because it is not uncommon for AI to present a guess with confidence. A speaker's name can appear three ways in one document. A figure can be off by a digit. A reader who knows the field will catch the error and trust the author a little less.

Transcripts and the summaries produced by AI often lose context. Speakers joke, hedge, qualify and correct themselves. A person in the room hears the pause before an answer and the moment a panelist walks back a claim. A transcript flattens all of it, and someone has to decide what the speaker meant before it is published under the name of the firm.

Similarly, technology will gloss over some of the details and anecdotes a human reader may find interesting. The finished product assembled by the AI may include an exhaustive summary, but it will often miss some of the points and insights that made the conference worth having.

Selection is a key point in favor of hiring a writer. Choosing ideas that could resonate and deleting other information is an editorial judgment about an audience. This is more complex than a summarizing task and significantly, it’s essential for developing content that is engaging and easy to read.

Accountability is another factor that is worthy of consideration. A quote from a speaker or an interpretation of a regulation on the company’s letterhead creates obligations. Some remarks are made off the record or in a setting where the speaker would not expect to be quoted, and software has no way to tell the difference.

Fabrications and hallucinations bring legal risks. Tools that are tasked with building content from a transcript are focused on pleasing the user. The result is that AI will occasionally fill gaps with plausible text that was never said, and a fluent error is harder to catch than a rough one.

These are a few of the reasons why my conference work begins in the room. I attend the sessions in person and record them, but I also listen carefully and take notes to ensure the accuracy of the finished product. Every name, figure and quote is checked against the recording before drafting, and the client reviews the draft before anything is published. Software speeds up the transcript, and a person takes responsibility for the article.

The method was developed for a regional law firm and applies to any field where the people in the room know things worth publishing, including real estate, finance, construction, healthcare, energy and professional associations.
excerpt: Transcription software has improved such that it is tempting to treat a conference as a solved problem. Why review the content or hire a writer if it isn't necessary?

title: How to Repurpose Content from Seminars and Conferences
html:
Hosting a client seminar or sending key people to a conference is expensive. The content that is produced by the subject matter experts at these events has already been paid for, so it is worth considering publishing it to foster engagement with existing clients, prospects and stakeholders.

In many cases, however, the content evaporates when the event is over. The raw material could be used on a variety of platforms, so it is easy to see the value in repurposing it.

Afterward, the raw material supports more formats than most firms expect. A single session could produce an in-depth article or client alert with timely updates and conversational insights from the speakers that are not available in other outlets.

Long-form content can be easily broken down into newsletter items, a series of LinkedIn posts or even a separate landing page for the business.

The raw material could be used to create a frequently asked questions page or an internal memo that captures the competitive intelligence the public pieces leave out.

Using the content to develop a pitch to a trade publication or local business journal is another high-value, low-effort idea that would represent a home run for the business if the article was published.

Repurposing the material requires some planning before the event, however, as a decision will need to be made about how to capture it effectively. Content from a seminar hosted by the company belongs to the business and can be freely used, subject to the speakers' approval.

A conference session delivered by someone else can be reported on and quoted with attribution. A best practice is to identify the sessions that may be interesting to clients in advance. The next step is to reach out to the speakers to ask permission.

During the event, record with permission and take notes anyway. The recording preserves the exact wording. The notes preserve the sequence of the speakers, questions from the audience and a variety of additional details that may not be easily understood by transcription software.

Quotes and figures should be reviewed against the recording. Similarly, any individual who is named in the article should have a chance to review the draft.

The timing is important because anything with recent updates could be viewed as news. The same article that is published after two months loses that advantage, as a competitor may have already published on the topic. The initial articles should be drafted while the session is fresh, and the speakers are still reachable for edits and approvals.

I developed this process for a regional law firm, attending seminars in person and turning the sessions into published articles. The same sequence applies to a real estate convention, a financial industry conference or an association's annual meeting, and a conversation before the next event is the easiest time to plan for it.
excerpt: Hosting a client seminar or sending key people to a conference is expensive. The content that is produced by the subject matter experts at these events has already been paid for, so it is worth considering publishing it to foster engagement with existing clients, prospects and stakeholders.

title: The Importance of Real Estate Articles in Marketing
html:
A real estate article positions the agent as an expert, building trust long before there is a reason to buy or sell. Most people spend months thinking about a move before they contact anyone, and during that period they read. The agent or brokerage whose explanations they keep finding becomes the one they call.

The subjects that earn that trust are usually practical. A plain account of local market conditions with inventory, pricing figures and analyses from industry experts is more useful than an ad or a slogan. A guide to the steps between an accepted offer and the closing becomes a useful resource for buyers. A neighborhood piece that explains school boundaries, commute times and what a budget actually buys tells a relocating family more than a dozen listings.

Market conditions set the agenda. When the data show first-time buyers returning to a region, articles on financing options and inspection basics become essential to the brokerage and its agents. Similarly, an article that outlines how to negotiate is timely when inventory tightens. The articles that perform the best answer questions people are actually asking.

Articles carry weight with search engines, but the mechanism is simpler than many people think. Search engines reward pages that answer specific questions clearly. An article explaining how property taxes are reassessed after a sale in a particular county will draw search traffic for years, long after a social media post on the same subject has disappeared from the feed. This is the holy grail that is often referred to as evergreen content.

A single well-made article can also feed countless other channels. It can be condensed into a newsletter, divided into a week of social posts, sent to a client for reference, or pitched to a local business journal as the basis for an article. The research is done once.

Content falls short for a variety of reasons. Some articles may go into too much detail about the agent instead of engaging the reader. Others may just reproduce what every other brokerage is already saying or read as generic marketing copy that was generated for the sole purpose of filling a calendar. A reader knows within a paragraph and so do the search engines.

As it is with many other things in life, the key is delivering value. Through market updates, process guides and neighborhood articles, I help agents and brokerages become an essential resource for current and prospective clients. Reach out if you’re ready to start building a library of content that shows the value and depth of the insights you offer.

title: What a Business Gains by Outsourcing Professional Writing
html:
Many professional services firms produce and distribute content that was created by someone who does not have the word writer in their job title. A managing partner may write a client alert late at night. A broker-owner may draft a newsletter between showings. An office manager may be asked to write a press release because of having prior experience at a newspaper.

The writing is done at a cost that is difficult to quantify. Judging the quality of the work is unfair to the writer if that person does not specialize in that area of business on a daily basis.

Outsourcing the work to a professional changes the math.

One reason is the hourly rate of the writer is typically lower than an attorney or managing broker, for example. An attorney who bills at $500 per hour and spends a few on an article has created a very expensive article. That is before counting client work that was displaced and/or opportunity costs. If an attorney hires a writer, the involvement that is required drops substantially, down to providing some information and a review of the draft.

A writer who has produced several hundred market updates or client alerts has already worked out the structure readers follow and the mistakes that lose them. A firm producing its first dozen is learning those lessons on the job.

Outsourcing content needs may also be preferable to hiring someone to work on staff. A staff writer's salary and benefits are fixed whether the month is profitable or not. An outside writer is paid for the work that is produced, which is often a better fit for a brokerage with needs that spike around market reports and new listings, or a law firm with content needs that revolve around the latest updates in the legal field.

An outside writer can also make complex ideas more approachable to the average person. An expert who is already in the business may use jargon and terms that are only recognizable to their peers and colleagues. An outside writer asks the questions a prospective client would ask and clearly explains technical ideas, such that the article is easy to read and informative.

Ongoing engagements allow the writer to make a lasting, positive impact on the organization. A writer can build a thorough knowledge of a client’s business over time, adapting content and style to the strategy, processes and people. The time and effort involved with onboarding is only paid once. As a writer for Berkshire Hathaway HomeServices California Properties since 2008, I have become a trusted resource for the brokerage and the agents it serves.

Outsourcing does not eliminate responsibility for substance or accuracy. The attorney still supplies the analysis, the broker still supplies the market read, and the person whose name is on the piece still reviews every word before it is published. The writer's contribution is the structure, the clarity and time, and a good engagement is honest about that division from the first call.

If you’re curious about how this would work or have any questions, please reach out.

title: Professional Copywriter, In-House Writer, or AI Tool: What a Business Gets from Each
html:
A business that needs content can essentially choose from three options: assign it to a person on staff, generate it with AI or hire a professional copywriter. Each produces a different result, of course, and a simple cost/benefit analysis can make it easier to choose between which option supports the needs of the business in the best possible way.

Writing in house has the advantage of proximity. The person doing the work understands the business, can walk down the hall to check a fact and turn a piece around the same day. The downside is that the writing is usually assigned to someone with many other responsibilities, so the work is typically low on the list of priorities. The quality may vary depending on the workflow of the week. Also, an internal writer may use terms and jargon that are difficult for outsiders to understand.

AI tools are faster and cheaper. A tool can produce a competent, grammatical draft on almost any subject in seconds, and for an internal summary or a first pass that might be enough. The limits are clear in a closer review, however. A tool does not interview anyone or brainstorm about additional details that could inform the content, so the finished product does not have new information. The fact that AI will fill gaps with generalities, invent statistics or regulations to support a conclusion is even more concerning. Further, AI takes no responsibility for mistakes and negative outcomes produced by those mistakes. Readers can immediately spot AI-generated material and business may receive a harsh judgment for using it.

A business that chooses a professional copywriter is looking for craft and accountability. The writer begins with research and interviews to uncover new information and details that will be positively impactful to the business. A writer with experience understands the target audience and the importance of researching stated claims. And perhaps most importantly, the reputation of the writer is attached to the result even when the byline belongs to the client. A writer will be more expensive and need more time compared to other options, but for businesses that value quality and accountability, the choice is clear.

Leveraging each option may deliver a competitive advantage for some businesses. Staff handle routine internal communications, tools handle summaries and drafts that outsiders never see, and a professional writer handles the content that could positively or negatively impact the reputation of the business: the website, thought leadership, the press releases, newsletters—basically anything a client or a regulator might read.

My work is mainly focused on quality and accountability over speed, but if you’re looking for someone to help review your AI-generated content, I am open to ideas and the word ‘No’ is not in my vocabulary when it comes to discussing a project with a client.

title: What Impact Can Charitable Initiatives Have on Real Estate Development and Community Engagement?
html:
A real estate development changes the landscape of a community dramatically, and a developer that does not consider the potential negative impacts to the neighborhood is certain to face a significant amount of backlash from the residents. Adding a charitable initiative to a project can reduce this backlash, further the interests of the developer and help the community, creating a win-win for everyone involved.

There are a variety of methods for achieving this objective. A developer could donate to a local school, establish a long-term partnership with a housing nonprofit, build a trail system, set aside open space, or make ongoing contributions to community organizations. The options are only limited to the imagination of the people involved.

Residents who oppose a project usually oppose what they expect to lose: parking, green space, a view, the character of a street. A development that commits to a public park, a library branch or a community room gives neighbors something concrete to weigh against those losses, and it gives the planning board a record of enforceable commitments. Town hall meetings can assist in the approval process, as residents value having a chance to review the plans and ask for changes.

Buyers, community stakeholders and tenants increasingly consider the actions, or inactions, of a developer and/or brokerage beyond the transaction. Community features that are built and maintained instead of just promised can become a part of the sales presentation. The residents who use them serve as a credible advocate for the developer and the project.

Housing affordability is another critical issue. Partnerships with nonprofits focused on affordable housing allow a developer to include a range of price points in a project. Mixed-income developments are more complex to finance and manage, however, these projects answer the affordability question that now follows nearly every new project through the approval process.

At the brokerage level, charitable involvement creates a positive touch point with the local community. An office that sponsors a fundraiser, a team that volunteers with a local charity or an agent who donates a portion of each commission builds the kind of local standing that produces referrals.

Communicating these efforts is a separate matter, and it is where many well-intended programs fall short. A charitable initiative described in the language of a marketing campaign reads as a marketing campaign. A press release about a fundraiser should name the organization, state what was raised or built, credit the people who did the work and stop.

If you’re looking for an announcement that will support your business as well as the cause that is important to you, please reach out.
